glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Matthew introduces Jesus Christ as the Son of David and the Son of Abraham through a carefully arranged genealogy, then tells of His conception by the Holy Spirit and His naming as the Savior who is Immanuel, “God with us.”

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 1 opens the New Testament and the first movement of Matthew’s Gospel, The Promised King Comes (1:1–4:16), which sets out who Jesus is before He begins to preach.

glance.label: Chapter Outline

  • Matthew 1:18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And she will bring forth a Son, and you shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins.” (Matthew 1:21, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Matthew’s first sentence tells the reader what the whole Gospel will prove: Jesus Christ is “the Son of David, the Son of Abraham” (1:1). David points to the throne God promised would last forever; Abraham points to the promise that all nations would be blessed through his family. Before Jesus says a word, Matthew places Him at the meeting point of both promises.

The genealogy that follows is history arranged with purpose. Matthew sets it in three groups of fourteen generations, from Abraham to David, from David to the deportation to Babylon, and from Babylon to the Christ (1:17). The line rises to a king, falls into exile and then waits, and the waiting ends in Jesus. Along the way Matthew names women an ancient record could easily have left out: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and “her who had been the wife of Uriah” (1:6). Their stories hold scandal, grief, outsiders brought in, and the surprising providence of God. Then the pattern breaks. After the long chain of “begot,” Matthew writes that Joseph was “the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus” (1:16). Joseph gives Jesus his royal line; he does not give Him life.

The birth account explains why. Mary is “found with child of the Holy Spirit” (1:18). Joseph, “a just man” (1:19), plans to end the betrothal quietly, until God speaks to him through an angel in a dream. He obeys, takes Mary home and names the child Jesus, “for He will save His people from their sins” (1:21). Matthew sees in all this the fulfillment of Isaiah’s word that the virgin would bear a Son called Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23). The Savior of sinners is God Himself come to be with His people, and Matthew’s Gospel will end with the same promise, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 1:1–17 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ

Matthew traces Jesus’ ancestry from Abraham through David and the exile to Joseph, arranging it in three groups of fourteen so that Israel’s whole history leads to the Christ. The names include kings and ordinary men, faithful and unfaithful, and four women before Mary whose stories show God’s grace working through unlikely people.

Matthew 1:18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ

Mary is found with child by the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph come together, and Joseph, a just man, is redirected by an angel in a dream to take her as his wife. He obeys and names the child Jesus, the Savior from sins, in fulfillment of the prophecy of Immanuel, “God with us.”

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 1 shows that Jesus did not appear out of nowhere. God had made promises to Abraham and David and carried them through centuries of faithfulness and failure, exile and silence, until they met in one Person. The Christian faith rests on what God did in history, and this chapter puts names and generations to it.

The chapter also shows the kind of salvation Jesus brings. The angel does not say He will free Israel from Rome, but that He will save His people from their sins, and Matthew adds that in Him God is with us. The family line, with its outsiders and broken stories, already shows a God who works His purposes through people who could not earn a place in them.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Promise kept. Jesus is the heir of the promises to David and Abraham, and history moves toward Him (1:1, 17).

Grace in the family line. Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba show God working through unexpected people and histories (1:3, 5–6).

The work of the Holy Spirit. Jesus’ conception is “of the Holy Spirit,” a true miracle (1:18, 20).

Obedient faith. Joseph receives God’s word in a dream and does exactly what he is told (1:19–20, 24–25).

God with us. The names Jesus and Immanuel reveal who He is and what He came to do (1:21–23).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Son of David, Son of Abraham. Titles of descent, not immediate parentage. David points to Jesus as the promised King, Abraham to the promise of blessing for all nations (1:1).

Fourteen. Matthew’s structuring number (1:17). The Hebrew consonants of David’s name add up to fourteen (D-W-D, 4 + 6 + 4), which may reinforce the Davidic emphasis, though Matthew does not explain the number. Like other biblical genealogies, the list may pass over some generations.

The women. Tamar (Genesis 38), Rahab of Jericho (Joshua 2), Ruth the Moabite and Bathsheba, “her who had been the wife of Uriah” (1:6). Matthew identifies Bathsheba as Uriah’s wife without giving her personal name. He gives no single reason for naming these women, but two came from outside Israel and each story shows God’s providence. Mary is the fifth woman mentioned in the genealogy (1:16), and the change in wording at her name sets her apart from the others.

Betrothed. A binding commitment before the couple lived together, so that Joseph is already called Mary’s husband and could end it only by divorce (1:18–19).

Jesus. The Greek form of Joshua, a name meaning the LORD saves, explained by the angel: “He will save His people from their sins” (1:21).

Immanuel. A Hebrew name from Isaiah 7:14 meaning “God with us” (1:23). Matthew presents it as fulfilled in Jesus’ birth and as a statement of who He is.

focus: Matthew 1 introduces Jesus Christ as the Son of David and the Son of Abraham through a structured genealogy, then tells of His conception by the Holy Spirit and His birth, revealing Him as the Savior who will save His people from their sins and as Immanuel, “God with us.”

sections.title: The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
sections.summary: Matthew traces Jesus’ ancestry from Abraham through David and the deportation to Babylon to Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born. He arranges the generations in three groups of fourteen.

sections.title: The Birth of Jesus Christ
sections.summary: Before Mary and Joseph come together, she is found with child of the Holy Spirit, and an angel of the Lord tells Joseph, a just man, to take her as his wife and to call the Son Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins. Matthew identifies this as the fulfillment of the prophecy that the virgin would bear a Son called Immanuel, and Joseph obeys and names the child Jesus.

1.brief: Matthew opens by naming Jesus Christ “the Son of David, the Son of Abraham.” From the first line he presents Jesus as the King promised to David and the descendant through whom God would bless all nations as He promised Abraham.
1.explain:
“The book of the genealogy”

The word translated “genealogy” means “origin” or “beginning,” and it is the word from which the book of Genesis takes its name. The expression echoes Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, where the same wording introduces the account of the heavens and the earth and the family line of Adam. Matthew begins the New Testament the way Genesis began the Old, with an account of origins. With the coming of Jesus, God is making a new beginning in His dealings with humanity.

“of Jesus Christ,”

“Jesus” is His personal name, and the angel will explain its meaning in 1:21. “Christ” is a title. It comes from the Greek word for “anointed one,” which translates the Hebrew word for Messiah. In the Old Testament, kings, priests, and at times prophets were anointed with oil to set them apart for their work. By Jesus’ day, “the Messiah” had come to mean the King God promised to send from David’s family to deliver His people. Matthew states this claim in his first line, and the rest of the Gospel shows why it is true.

“the Son of David,”

God promised David that one of his descendants would rule on his throne forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). The prophets developed this hope, speaking of a coming King from David’s line who would reign in righteousness (Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1–10; Jeremiah 23:5–6). “Son of David” therefore became a way of saying “the Messiah.” “Son” here means descendant, since David lived about a thousand years before Jesus. Matthew uses the title more than any other Gospel writer. Blind men, a Canaanite mother, and the Jerusalem crowds will all call out to Jesus by this name (9:27; 15:22; 21:9).

“the Son of Abraham:”

Abraham is the father of the Jewish people. When God called him, He promised, “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3; see also 22:18). As the Son of Abraham, Jesus is the true heir of that promise, and through Him its blessing reaches the nations. Matthew’s Gospel begins with Abraham and ends with Jesus sending His disciples to “make disciples of all the nations” (28:19).

Matthew names David before Abraham, even though Abraham lived nearly a thousand years earlier. The order highlights kingship. Jesus is first of all the promised King. The genealogy that follows then moves in historical order from Abraham to David and on to Christ.
1.notes:
David’s reign is conventionally dated about 1010–970 BC.

The Greek phrase biblos geneseōs, “the book of the genealogy,” appears in exactly this form in the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1.

Interpreters debate whether Matthew intends it as a heading for the genealogy alone (1:2–17), for the birth narrative (chapters 1–2), or for the entire Gospel. It most naturally introduces the genealogy.

In the critical Greek text the same word reappears in 1:18 (“birth”), linking the genealogy and the birth account. The manuscripts the NKJV follows read the closely related gennēsis there.

Jewish genealogies established identity, inheritance, and the right to hold certain offices. After the exile, men who could not prove their priestly descent from the records were excluded from the priesthood (Ezra 2:59–63).

The historian Josephus, writing later in the first century, records his own priestly descent from public registers. For anyone presented as the Messiah, descent from David was essential.

Matthew uses the title “Son of David” about ten times, more than Mark and Luke combined. Apart from 1:20, where the angel addresses Joseph, it always refers to Jesus.

2.brief: The record begins with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the patriarchs who received God’s promise, and then names Judah and his brothers. Judah’s mention prepares for the royal line, since kingship in Israel would come through his tribe.
2.explain:
“Abraham begot Isaac,”

“Begot” means “became the father of.” The NKJV keeps the traditional word, which Matthew repeats through 1:16 like a steady drumbeat. Isaac was the child of promise, born when Abraham and Sarah were far past the age of having children (Genesis 18:11–14; 21:1–3). From the first step, the Messiah’s line depended on God’s power. God chose Isaac rather than Ishmael, Abraham’s older son, as the heir of the promise (Genesis 17:19–21).

“Isaac begot Jacob,”

Jacob was the younger of Isaac’s twin sons. Before the twins were born, God declared that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23). God later renamed Jacob “Israel” (Genesis 32:28), and the nation descended from him bears that name.

“and Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.”

Judah was Jacob’s fourth son by Leah (Genesis 29:35). Reuben, the firstborn, lost his privileged place because of his sin (Genesis 49:3–4; 1 Chronicles 5:1–2). On his deathbed Jacob prophesied that “the scepter shall not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10), marking Judah as the tribe of Israel’s kings. David and every king of Judah came from this tribe.

“And his brothers” refers to the twelve sons of Jacob, the fathers of Israel’s twelve tribes. The line of the Messiah narrows to one tribe, but Matthew keeps the whole family of Israel in view. The King who comes from Judah comes for all of God’s people.
2.notes: The Greek verb gennaō, “begot,” appears in the active form thirty-nine times in 1:2–16. In biblical genealogies it can describe descent across more than one generation, so that A begot B may mean A was the ancestor of B. This usage becomes important in 1:8 and 1:11. In 1:16 the pattern changes.

3.brief: Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and the line continues through Hezron and Ram. Naming Tamar recalls the painful story of Genesis 38, where Judah wronged her, and shows God carrying His promise forward through a family history marked by failure.
3.explain:
“Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar,”

Tamar was Judah’s daughter-in-law. After her first two husbands, Judah’s sons Er and Onan, died under God’s judgment, Judah promised her his third son, Shelah, and then failed to keep his word. Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute, and Judah, not recognizing her, fathered twins by her. When the truth came out, Judah confessed, “She has been more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26). Judah’s own confession places the greater blame on himself.

Ancient genealogies normally traced descent through fathers, and Matthew could easily have left Tamar’s name out. He includes her, the first of four women named before Mary. Matthew records the troubling parts of Israel’s history openly. The Messiah’s family tree includes deception, sin, and broken promises, and God still carried His purpose forward through it.

Perez and Zerah were twins. At their birth Perez broke through ahead of his brother, and his name means “breach” or “breaking through” (Genesis 38:27–30). The line continues through Perez, whose descendants became the leading clan of Judah. When the elders of Bethlehem blessed Boaz and Ruth, they prayed that their house would be “like the house of Perez” (Ruth 4:12).

“Perez begot Hezron, and Hezron begot Ram.”

Hezron was among the members of Jacob’s family who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:12). From this point through 1:6, Matthew follows the family record of Judah preserved in Ruth 4:18–22 and 1 Chronicles 2:5–15.
3.notes:
Zerah’s descendants formed the Zerahite clan of Judah, which included Achan (Numbers 26:20; Joshua 7:1).

Matthew names four women in the genealogy: Tamar (1:3), Rahab (1:5), Ruth (1:5), and “her who had been the wife of Uriah” (1:6), and later Mary (1:16). He does not state a single reason for including them, and interpreters have noted several features.

Three of the four stories involve sin or scandal: Judah’s relations with Tamar, Rahab’s life as a prostitute before she came to faith, and David’s adultery with Bathsheba.

Several of the women also had connections with the Gentile world: Rahab was a Canaanite and Ruth a Moabitess; Tamar’s nationality is not stated, though the setting of Genesis 38 suggests she was a Canaanite; and Bathsheba was married to Uriah the Hittite.

Their histories differ widely. Tamar was wronged and responded with deception; Rahab was a prostitute who came to faith; Ruth was a woman of loyal and godly character; and Bathsheba was taken by a king who then had her husband killed. Mary’s place in 1:16 stands apart from all of them, since her Son was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

For Abraham to David, Matthew’s list agrees with the Old Testament genealogies in Ruth 4:18–22 and 1 Chronicles 1:34; 2:1–15. The Greek spellings of several names follow the Septuagint.

4.brief: The line passes through Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, and Salmon. Nahshon was a leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, so these names carry the family from Egypt toward the land God promised.
4.explain:
“Ram begot Amminadab,”

Little is known about Ram. His son Amminadab is mentioned in Exodus 6:23, where his daughter Elisheba marries Aaron, Moses’ brother. The family of Judah’s future kings was joined by marriage to the family of Israel’s high priests.

“Amminadab begot Nahshon,”

Nahshon was the leader of the tribe of Judah during the wilderness years (Numbers 1:7; 2:3). When the tabernacle was dedicated, he was the first of the tribal leaders to bring an offering (Numbers 7:12). When Israel broke camp, Judah’s standard went first, with Nahshon at its head (Numbers 10:14). Long before Israel had a king, the tribe of Judah was already leading God’s people.

“and Nahshon begot Salmon.”

Salmon belongs to the generation that entered Canaan under Joshua. Matthew 1:5 connects him with Rahab of Jericho, placing him at the time of Israel’s first victory in the land.
4.notes:
Israel lived in Egypt for 430 years (Exodus 12:40), yet only a few generations are named between Hezron, who entered Egypt, and Nahshon, who left it. Likewise, only four names (Salmon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse) span the long period from the conquest to David.

Biblical genealogies often skip generations and focus on key ancestors. Matthew is following the Old Testament lists here; his own deliberate omissions come later (1:8, 11).

1 Chronicles 2:11 spells the name Salmon “Salma,” and Ruth 4:20–21 uses both “Salmon” and “Salmah” in the Hebrew. These are variant spellings of the same name.

5.brief: Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, and Obed fathered Jesse. Rahab of Jericho and Ruth the Moabite were both outsiders welcomed into Israel, and their place in the King’s family displays God’s grace reaching beyond Israel’s borders.
5.explain:
“Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab,”

Rahab was the prostitute of Jericho who hid Israel’s spies and confessed, “The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). She belonged to a Canaanite city under God’s judgment, yet because she trusted the God of Israel, she and her household were spared when Jericho fell (Joshua 6:22–25). The New Testament honors her for both her faith (Hebrews 11:31) and her actions (James 2:25). The Old Testament does not record her marriage, but Matthew tells us she married Salmon and became the mother of Boaz.

“Boaz begot Obed by Ruth,”

Ruth was a widow from Moab, a nation that descended from Lot and had long been hostile to Israel. Moabites were barred from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3). Yet Ruth bound herself to her mother-in-law Naomi and to Naomi’s God: “Your people shall be my people, and your God, my God” (Ruth 1:16). Boaz, a man of Bethlehem, acted as her kinsman-redeemer, married her, and preserved the family line (Ruth 4:9–13). The story of Ruth ends by naming her son Obed as the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17).

Boaz was himself the son of a woman from outside Israel. The man who welcomed and redeemed a Moabite widow had grown up in a home where his own mother had once been a stranger to Israel’s God.

“Obed begot Jesse,”

Jesse lived in Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:1), the town of Boaz and Ruth. Isaiah prophesied that “a Rod from the stem of Jesse” would come forth, a descendant on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest (Isaiah 11:1–2). The mention of Jesse prepares the way for David in 1:6 and, more distantly, for the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem (2:1).
5.notes:
Matthew is the only biblical writer who connects Rahab with Salmon. His Greek spelling of her name (Rhachab) differs slightly from the spelling in Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25 (Rhaab), but both represent the same Hebrew name. Nothing in the text suggests a different woman.

Salmon belonged to the generation of the conquest and Boaz lived in the period of the judges. Like Ruth 4:20–22, this part of the genealogy may not record every generation, and the chronology of these years is difficult to establish precisely.

Deuteronomy 23:3 excluded Moabites from the assembly “even to the tenth generation.” Later Jewish teaching applied the restriction to Moabite men but not women (Mishnah, Yevamot 8:3).

6.brief: Jesse fathered “David the king,” the high point of the first part of the record, and David fathered Solomon by “her who had been the wife of Uriah.” Matthew identifies Bathsheba through Uriah, recalling David’s grievous sin, yet God kept His promise through Solomon.
6.explain:
“and Jesse begot David the king.”

David is the only person in the genealogy called “the king,” even though many of the names that follow belonged to kings. The title marks David as the high point of the first period of Israel’s history (1:17). He was the youngest of Jesse’s sons, a shepherd overlooked even by his own father (1 Samuel 16:11), yet God chose him and promised that his house and kingdom would be established forever (2 Samuel 7:16).

“David the king begot Solomon”

Matthew repeats “David the king,” keeping the royal theme in view. God chose Solomon to succeed David and to build the temple (1 Chronicles 22:9–10; 28:5–6).

“by her who had been the wife of Uriah.”

Matthew does not name Bathsheba. He identifies her by her first husband. Uriah the Hittite was one of David’s mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39). David committed adultery with Uriah’s wife and then arranged for Uriah to die in battle (2 Samuel 11). Scripture places the responsibility on David: “The thing that David had done displeased the LORD” (2 Samuel 11:27). By naming Uriah, Matthew brings David’s sin into the record of the Messiah’s ancestry.

Yet God’s mercy is also in view. After David repented, God gave him and Bathsheba another son, Solomon, and “the LORD loved him” (2 Samuel 12:24). The line of the Messiah continued through the child of a marriage that began in sin, after that sin had been confessed and forgiven.
6.notes:
Solomon’s reign is usually dated about 970–930 BC (dates approximate).

The phrase “her who had been the wife of Uriah” keeps Uriah, a Gentile soldier, in view. Nathan’s rebuke centered on David’s wrong against him (2 Samuel 12:9–10).

Bathsheba herself was the daughter of Eliam (2 Samuel 11:3), probably an Israelite. Her connection with the Gentile world comes through her marriage to Uriah.

Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry through Nathan, another son of David and Bathsheba (Luke 3:31; 1 Chronicles 3:5), rather than through Solomon. Matthew follows the royal line of kings who actually reigned.

7.brief: The royal line continues through Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, and Asa. Under Rehoboam the kingdom divided, and these kings carry the promise forward through a mixed history of faithfulness and failure.
7.explain:
“Solomon begot Rehoboam,”

Rehoboam’s harsh answer to the people’s request for relief split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:1–20). Ten tribes followed Jeroboam and formed the northern kingdom of Israel. Only Judah and Benjamin remained loyal to David’s house, which God preserved “for the sake of My servant David” (1 Kings 11:13). From this point on, Matthew’s list follows the kings of Judah.

“Rehoboam begot Abijah,”

Abijah “walked in all the sins of his father” (1 Kings 15:3). Yet Scripture adds, “for David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, by setting up his son after him” (1 Kings 15:4). The line continued because of God’s promise to David.

“and Abijah begot Asa.”

Asa “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as did his father David” (1 Kings 15:11). He removed idols and even deposed his grandmother for her idolatry. Later in his reign, however, he relied on the king of Syria rather than on the LORD and, when diseased, sought physicians rather than God (2 Chronicles 16:7–12). The problem was not that Asa received medical care, but that in his illness he relied on human help without seeking the LORD. Like many in this list, Asa’s life combined genuine faith with serious failure.
7.notes:
Rehoboam reigned about 930–913 BC, Abijah (called Abijam in 1 Kings 15:1–8) about 913–910 BC, and Asa about 910–869 BC. Dates are approximate, and some reigns overlapped through co-regencies.

Several of the oldest Greek manuscripts of Matthew read “Asaph” (the name of the psalmist) in 1:7–8, while most manuscripts read “Asa.” The NKJV follows “Asa.” Either way, the king of Judah is meant.

“Asaph” may reflect an alternate spelling or an early copying error. A similar variant appears in 1:10.

8.brief: Asa fathered Jehoshaphat, and the line moves through Joram to Uzziah. Matthew passes over several kings between Joram and Uzziah, showing that his record is a selected arrangement rather than a complete list of every generation.
8.explain:
“Asa begot Jehoshaphat,”

Jehoshaphat was a godly king who sent officials and Levites throughout Judah to teach the Book of the Law (2 Chronicles 17:7–9). He made one costly mistake: he allied himself with Ahab, the wicked king of Israel, and sealed the alliance by marriage (2 Chronicles 18:1; 19:2).

“Jehoshaphat begot Joram,”

Joram (also called Jehoram) married Ahab’s daughter Athaliah and “walked in the way of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done” (2 Kings 8:18). Yet Scripture again records that “the LORD would not destroy Judah, for the sake of His servant David” (2 Kings 8:19). The consequences of this marriage nearly ended David’s line. After Joram’s son died, Athaliah seized the throne and tried to destroy the entire royal family. Only one infant, Joash, survived, hidden in the temple for six years (2 Kings 11:1–3).

“and Joram begot Uzziah.”

Uzziah was not Joram’s son but his great-great-grandson. Between them stood three kings: Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah (1 Chronicles 3:11–12). Matthew passes over them and uses “begot” in the sense of “was the ancestor of.” Matthew is arranging Judah’s history according to the pattern he describes in 1:17.

Uzziah, also called Azariah, reigned fifty-two years and prospered while he sought the LORD. But when he became strong, his heart was lifted up, and he entered the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for the priests. God struck him with leprosy, and he lived in isolation until his death (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). It was “in the year that King Uzziah died” that Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1).
8.notes:
Jehoshaphat reigned about 872–848 BC, Joram (also called Jehoram) about 848–841 BC, and Uzziah about 792–740 BC, including co-regencies.

Matthew does not explain why Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah are left out. The clearest reason is structural: the omission keeps the second period at fourteen generations (1:17).

Some interpreters add that these three were the descendants of Athaliah, Ahab’s daughter, and suggest an allusion to God’s visiting iniquity “to the third and fourth generations” (Exodus 20:5). This is possible but not stated. All three kings died violently (2 Kings 9:27; 12:20–21; 14:19).

The names Uzziah and Azariah refer to the same king (2 Kings 15:1–7; 2 Chronicles 26:1–23). Both are built on Hebrew words for the LORD’s help or strength.

9.brief: Uzziah’s line continues through Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Ahaz was the unfaithful king to whom Isaiah first spoke the Immanuel sign, and his son Hezekiah led a return to the LORD, so the line holds both rebellion and reform.
9.explain:
“Uzziah begot Jotham,”

Jotham “did what was right in the sight of the LORD,” though “still the people acted corruptly” (2 Chronicles 27:2). He served as regent while his father Uzziah lived in isolation (2 Kings 15:5).

“Jotham begot Ahaz,”

Ahaz was one of the worst kings in Judah’s history. He worshiped the gods of the nations, made his son pass through the fire in pagan sacrifice (2 Kings 16:3), and eventually shut the doors of the temple (2 Chronicles 28:24).

Ahaz is especially significant for Matthew 1. When the kings of Syria and Israel threatened Jerusalem, Isaiah came to Ahaz with God’s promise of protection and invited him to ask for a sign. Ahaz refused, hiding his unbelief behind pious words. Isaiah then addressed the whole royal family: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and shall call His name Immanuel” (Isaiah 7:13–14). Instead of trusting the LORD, Ahaz sent silver and gold to the king of Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:7–8). The sign first given to the house of David in the days of its faithless king finds its fulfillment in that same house, in the birth of Jesus (1:23).

“and Ahaz begot Hezekiah.”

Hezekiah stands in sharp contrast to his father. He reopened and cleansed the temple, restored the Passover, and tore down the high places. Scripture says of him, “He trusted in the LORD God of Israel, so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor who were before him” (2 Kings 18:5). When the Assyrian army surrounded Jerusalem, Hezekiah spread the enemy’s letter before the LORD in prayer, and God delivered the city (2 Kings 19:14–36).
9.notes: Jotham reigned about 750–732 BC, Ahaz about 735–715 BC, and Hezekiah about 715–686 BC. The overlaps reflect co-regencies.

10.brief: Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, then come Amon and Josiah. Manasseh led Judah into deep idolatry, while Josiah later restored the worship of the LORD, and God’s promise endured through both.
10.explain:
“Hezekiah begot Manasseh,”

Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, longer than any other king of Judah. He rebuilt the pagan shrines his father had torn down, set up a carved image in the temple, practiced sorcery, sacrificed his son, and “shed very much innocent blood” (2 Kings 21:1–16). Second Kings records that his sins brought God’s sentence of judgment on Jerusalem, a sentence that still stood after Josiah’s reforms (2 Kings 21:10–15; 23:26; 24:3–4).

Second Chronicles adds the rest of Manasseh’s story. Taken captive to Babylon by the Assyrians, he “humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers” and prayed, and God heard him and restored him to Jerusalem. Manasseh then removed the foreign gods and the idol from the temple and commanded Judah to serve the LORD (2 Chronicles 33:11–16). The worst king in Judah’s history became a living witness that God receives those who truly repent.

“Manasseh begot Amon,”

Amon followed Manasseh’s early idolatry but not his repentance. He “did not humble himself before the LORD, as his father Manasseh had humbled himself” (2 Chronicles 33:23). His own servants killed him after two years (2 Kings 21:19–23).

“and Amon begot Josiah.”

Josiah became king at eight years old. During the repair of the temple, the Book of the Law was found, and Josiah responded by leading Judah in repentance, destroying idols throughout the land, and keeping a great Passover (2 Kings 22–23). Scripture says, “Now before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his might” (2 Kings 23:25). God had foretold Josiah’s reforms by name three centuries earlier (1 Kings 13:2).
10.notes:
Manasseh reigned about 697–642 BC (including a co-regency), Amon about 642–640 BC, and Josiah about 640–609 BC.

Kings and Chronicles give complementary accounts of Manasseh. Kings focuses on the effect of his reign on the nation and explains why judgment came on Judah despite Josiah’s reforms (2 Kings 23:26–27). Chronicles records Manasseh’s personal repentance and restoration.

As with “Asa” in 1:7–8, several early manuscripts read “Amos” rather than “Amon.” The NKJV follows “Amon,” the king named in 2 Kings 21:18. The variant is likely a spelling difference or an early copying error.

11.brief: Josiah’s line reaches Jeconiah and his brothers about the time Judah was carried away to Babylon. The exile marks the second turning point in the record, when David’s throne fell and the royal promise seemed to have failed.
11.explain:
“Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers”

Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin and Coniah, was Josiah’s grandson. His father Jehoiakim stands between them (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). As in 1:8, “begot” describes descent rather than a direct father-son relationship. After Josiah’s death, three of his sons and one grandson ruled in quick succession during Judah’s final years, all under the shadow of Egypt and Babylon.

“And his brothers” echoes “Judah and his brothers” in 1:2. In the first period, the family of Israel went down into Egypt. Here, at the close of the second period, the royal family goes into captivity in Babylon.

“about the time they were carried away to Babylon.”

In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah, his mother, his officials, and thousands of Judah’s leading citizens and craftsmen to Babylon (2 Kings 24:10–16). Eleven years later, in 586 BC, the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and the temple (2 Kings 25). Scripture presents the exile as God’s judgment for generations of idolatry and rebellion (2 Kings 24:3–4; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16). From that time on, no descendant of David sat on a throne in Jerusalem. The exile seemed to bring God’s promise of an everlasting throne to an end.
11.notes:
Jeconiah’s three-month reign fell in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8–15).

1 Chronicles 3:15–16 lists Josiah’s sons (Johanan, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum) and Jehoiakim’s sons (Jeconiah and another Zedekiah). Because Matthew has compressed the genealogy at this point by omitting Jehoiakim, the precise identification of “his brothers” is difficult. The expression appears to keep the wider royal family associated with the exile in view.

A few later manuscripts insert Jehoiakim between Josiah and Jeconiah, but the best-attested text does not include him.

The Greek word behind “carried away,” metoikesia, means “deportation” or removal to another place. Matthew uses it four times in 1:11–17, making the exile one of the three markers in his outline of Israel’s history.

12.brief: After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel. Even in exile the line of David continued, and Zerubbabel later led returning exiles and the rebuilding of the temple.
12.explain:
“And after they were brought to Babylon,”

The third period of Israel’s history begins in captivity. David’s descendants now lived as exiles in a foreign land. Jeconiah spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison before a new king released him and gave him a place at the royal table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27–30). Second Kings ends with this small act of kindness toward David’s heir, a quiet indication that God had not finished with David’s house.

“Jeconiah begot Shealtiel,”

Through Jeremiah, God had pronounced a severe judgment on Jeconiah: “Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not prosper in his days; for none of his descendants shall prosper, sitting on the throne of David” (Jeremiah 22:30). The judgment was real. Jeconiah had children (1 Chronicles 3:17), but he was recorded as “childless” in the sense that none of his sons would reign. No descendant of Jeconiah ever ruled as king in Jerusalem. Yet his family line continued.

“and Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel.”

Zerubbabel led the first group of exiles back to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:2) and served as governor of Judah under the Persians (Haggai 1:1). He laid the foundation of the second temple, and God promised he would complete it (Zechariah 4:9). Through Haggai, God spoke to him: “and will make you like a signet ring; for I have chosen you” (Haggai 2:23). A signet ring carried a king’s authority. God had once said that even if Jeconiah were the signet ring on His right hand, He would pull him off (Jeremiah 22:24). Now He uses the same picture to restore honor to Jeconiah’s grandson.

Zerubbabel never became king. He governed a small province under a foreign empire. The promise spoken to him pointed beyond his own life to the greater Son of David who was still to come.
12.notes:
Ezra, Nehemiah, and Haggai consistently call Zerubbabel “the son of Shealtiel” (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1). 1 Chronicles 3:17–19, however, lists him as the son of Pedaiah, Shealtiel’s brother.

Possible explanations include a levirate marriage, in which Pedaiah fathered a son on behalf of his childless brother (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), or Zerubbabel being reckoned as Shealtiel’s legal heir. The text does not say which.

Luke’s genealogy also includes Shealtiel and Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27), though it names different ancestors before and after them.

13.brief: Zerubbabel’s descendants continue through Abiud, Eliakim, and Azor. These names do not appear in the Old Testament accounts, and the royal family now passes through generations with no throne.
13.explain:
“Zerubbabel begot Abiud,”

Abiud does not appear among the sons of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chronicles 3:19–20. From this point to the end of the genealogy, Matthew draws on records outside the Old Testament. Jewish families, especially those of priestly or royal descent, kept careful family records (Ezra 2:62). Records of this kind were preserved, although Matthew does not identify the specific source he used.

“Abiud begot Eliakim, and Eliakim begot Azor.”

Nothing more is known of these men. Their names are recorded only here. The Old Testament closes with Zerubbabel’s generation and the prophets who encouraged them. The heirs of David who followed lived in the period the Old Testament does not describe. God preserved the line through people whose lives left no other mark on the historical record.
13.notes:
This Eliakim is a different man from King Jehoiakim, whose name was originally Eliakim (2 Kings 23:34).

The early church historian Eusebius, quoting the third-century writer Julius Africanus, records a tradition that relatives of Jesus preserved their family genealogies and explained them to others (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 1.7). The tradition cannot be verified, but it fits the Jewish practice of keeping family records.

14.brief: The line continues through Azor, Zadok, Achim, and Eliud. Generation after generation, God preserved David’s family while it lived in obscurity.
14.explain:
“Azor begot Zadok,”

This Zadok is not the priest who served in David’s day (2 Samuel 8:17). He is an otherwise unknown descendant of David. During these generations Judah passed from Persian rule to the empire of Alexander the Great and his successors. In the second century BC the Maccabean revolt brought a period of independence under the Hasmonean family, priest-kings from the tribe of Levi, not Judah. In 63 BC Rome took control, and Herod, whose family was of Edomite descent, was later made king of Judea by the Romans.

“Zadok begot Achim, and Achim begot Eliud.”

Throughout these centuries the throne of Israel was held by foreign rulers, by a priestly family, and finally by Herod. No son of David reigned. Yet the line continued, and with it the promise God had sworn to David.
14.notes:
Jewish writings from the century before Christ show that the hope of a Davidic king remained alive. The Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC, prays that God would raise up their king, the son of David to rule over Israel (17:21). By the time of Jesus, many in Israel were looking for this King (Luke 2:25, 38).

Eusebius records Hegesippus’s report that Domitian questioned the grandsons of Jude, the Lord’s brother, because they were descendants of David (Ecclesiastical History 3.19–20).

15.brief: Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, and Matthan fathered Jacob. The record now stands one generation from Joseph, with the long wait for the promised King nearly over.
15.explain:
“Eliud begot Eleazar, Eleazar begot Matthan,”

The last generations before Joseph are, like those before them, otherwise unknown. Matthan was Joseph’s grandfather.

“and Matthan begot Jacob.”

Jacob was Joseph’s father. The genealogy that began with “Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob” now arrives at another Jacob on the threshold of the Messiah’s birth. In 1:16 the long pattern of fathers and sons will reach its final link and then change.
15.notes: Luke names Joseph’s father as Heli and his grandfather as Matthat (Luke 3:23–24). The similarity between Matthan and Matthat has led some interpreters to suggest the two lists converge here.

16.brief: Jacob fathered “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus who is called Christ.” Matthew breaks his pattern of fathers begetting sons, identifying Joseph as Mary’s husband and Jesus as born of Mary, which prepares for the account of His conception by the Holy Spirit.
16.explain:
“And Jacob begot Joseph”

The pattern continues one more time. Joseph is a descendant of David (1:20; Luke 1:27; 2:4), a carpenter by trade (13:55), living in the small town of Nazareth (Luke 1:26–27).

“the husband of Mary,”

Here the pattern breaks. Thirty-nine times Matthew has written that one man “begot” the next. He does not write, Joseph begot Jesus. Instead, he identifies Joseph by his relationship to Mary. Joseph is called Mary’s “husband” because their betrothal was a legally binding union (1:18).

“of whom was born Jesus”

In Greek, “of whom” is feminine. Jesus was born of Mary, not fathered by Joseph. The verb also changes. Instead of the active “begot,” Matthew uses the passive “was born,” pointing to an act of God that 1:18–25 will explain.

Joseph’s role is nevertheless essential. By taking Mary as his wife and naming her Son, Joseph publicly received Jesus as his son and brought Him into his household. Through Joseph, Jesus stood within the royal house of David, while Matthew makes equally clear that Joseph was not His biological father.

“who is called Christ.”

The genealogy ends where it began (1:1), with Jesus the Christ. “Who is called” means who is known as or who is acknowledged as. The long history from Abraham through David and the exile has reached its goal in Him.
16.notes:
In 1:16 the Greek ex hēs (“of whom”) is feminine singular, referring to Mary. The verb egennēthē (“was born”) is passive, in contrast to the thirty-nine active forms of “begot” before it. Interpreters often call this a “divine passive,” in which God is the unstated actor.

Luke’s genealogy (Luke 3:23–38) runs backward from Jesus to Adam, passes through David’s son Nathan rather than Solomon, and names Heli rather than Jacob as Joseph’s father. Three main explanations have been offered.

One view holds that Matthew gives Joseph’s legal or royal line, while Luke gives his natural descent.

Another holds that Luke gives Mary’s ancestry, with Heli as Mary’s father and Joseph as his son-in-law.

A third, recorded by Julius Africanus, holds that Jacob and Heli were half-brothers, and that a levirate marriage made Joseph the natural son of one and the legal son of the other.

Both genealogies place Jesus in the family of David.

17.brief: Matthew arranges the record into three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from the exile to the Christ. The deliberate arrangement shows Israel’s history moving under God’s hand toward the coming of the Messiah.
17.explain:
“So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations,”

Matthew now summarizes the genealogy. The first period moves from the promise given to Abraham to its first great fulfillment in David, the king. It is a story of rising hope.

“from David until the captivity in Babylon are fourteen generations,”

The second period begins at the height of the kingdom and ends in its collapse. The throne God promised to David was lost, and Judah was carried away.

“and from the captivity in Babylon until the Christ are fourteen generations.”

The third period moves from exile to the Messiah. The family that lost the throne is the family from which the true King comes. The phrase “the Christ” (with the article) names Jesus as the Messiah, the goal toward which the whole history has been moving.

Matthew’s arrangement is deliberate. The list passes over several generations (1:8, 11), and the result is three equal periods. The structure made the genealogy easy to remember and teach, and it makes a theological point. The repeated number keeps attention on David, whose name marks the turning point between the first two periods (see Study Notes). Through promise, kingdom, failure, and exile, God was ordering history toward the birth of His Son. Paul expresses the same truth: “When the fullness of the time had come, God sent forth His Son, born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4).
17.notes:
The first period (Abraham through David) contains fourteen names. If David is counted again as the first name of the second period, David through Josiah gives fourteen, and Jeconiah through Jesus gives fourteen.

Other ways of counting have been proposed, such as counting Jeconiah twice or counting Mary as a generation. Matthew does not explain his method.

Hebrew letters also served as numbers, and the consonants of David’s name (D-W-D) have the value 4 + 6 + 4 = 14, so the repeated number may reinforce Matthew’s presentation of Jesus as the Son of David.

Another possibility is that Matthew saw significance in fourteen as twice seven, a number associated in Scripture with completeness. Matthew does not explicitly identify either explanation.

Arranging genealogies in symmetrical patterns was not unusual. Genesis 5 and 11 each list ten generations, from Adam to Noah and from Shem to Abraham. Such patterns aided memory and highlighted significant figures without claiming to name every generation.

18.brief: Matthew now tells how the birth of Jesus Christ came about: Mary was betrothed to Joseph, and before they came together she was found with child “of the Holy Spirit.” Jesus’ conception was God’s own miraculous work, not the result of any human father.
18.explain:
“Now the birth of Jesus Christ was as follows:”

The word translated “birth” is the same word translated “genealogy” in 1:1. Matthew has shown that Jesus belongs to the family of David through Joseph. Now he explains how Jesus could be born into that family without Joseph being His father. Luke tells the story of Jesus’ birth largely from Mary’s side (Luke 1–2). Matthew tells it from Joseph’s.

“After His mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph,”

Jewish marriage took place in two stages. The first was betrothal, a formal and legally binding commitment made before witnesses. A betrothed couple were called husband and wife, and the relationship could be ended only by divorce. Unfaithfulness during betrothal was treated as adultery (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). The bride, however, normally remained in her father’s home, often for about a year. The second stage came when the husband brought his bride into his home, the marriage was celebrated, and the couple began living together. Mary and Joseph were in the first stage.

“before they came together,”

The phrase refers to the couple beginning their life together, including sexual union. Matthew states plainly that Mary’s pregnancy began before this. Joseph was not the father.

“she was found with child of the Holy Spirit.”

“Was found” means her pregnancy became evident. Matthew states at once what Joseph does not yet know: the child is “of the Holy Spirit.” Jesus’ conception was a creative act of God. Luke records the angel’s words to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Highest will overshadow you; therefore, also, that Holy One who is to be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). The Spirit who moved over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) now brings into being the life of the One through whom God will make all things new.

The virgin conception is essential to who Jesus is. He is truly human, “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4), and He is the eternal Son of God who took on human flesh (John 1:14). Scripture affirms both, and Matthew’s account shows both from the very beginning.
18.notes:
Later Jewish sources describe betrothal (erusin or kiddushin) as creating a legal marriage. If a betrothed man died, his betrothed was considered a widow. Ending the betrothal required a certificate of divorce, an application of the divorce law of Deuteronomy 24:1 found in later Jewish sources.

Girls were often betrothed young, commonly in their early to mid-teens, though Scripture does not give Mary’s age.

The Greek ek pneumatos hagiou (from the Holy Spirit) identifies the Spirit as the source of the conception. The same expression appears in 1:20, with “is” between the words.

19.brief: Joseph, Mary’s husband and “a just man,” did not want to make her a public example and resolved to divorce her quietly, since betrothal was a binding marriage covenant that could be ended only by divorce. His righteousness joined respect for God’s law with mercy toward Mary, before he knew the truth about the child.
19.explain:
“Then Joseph her husband,”

Joseph is called Mary’s “husband” because the betrothal was a binding union. Matthew does not record what Joseph concluded or how he felt, though the pregnancy would naturally have appeared to be unfaithfulness. The woman he had pledged to marry was carrying a child that was not his.

“being a just man,”

“Just” means righteous. In Scripture a righteous person is one who lives in faithful obedience to God and His law (Luke 1:6). The law treated unfaithfulness during betrothal as a serious sin (Deuteronomy 22:20–24). Matthew connects Joseph’s righteousness with his decision to end the betrothal.

“and not wanting to make her a public example,”

Joseph had another option. He could have accused Mary publicly and brought the matter before the elders, exposing her to disgrace. He chose not to. His righteousness was joined to mercy. He would act on what he believed was right, but he would not use the law to shame her.

“was minded to put her away secretly.”

“Was minded” means he had made up his mind. “Put her away” refers to divorce, the legal means of ending a betrothal. “Secretly” means quietly, without a public accusation. Matthew does not describe the procedure Joseph planned, but his intent was to end the betrothal with as little shame to Mary as possible.
19.notes:
Deuteronomy 22:23–24 prescribed death for a betrothed woman who willingly lay with another man. By the first century, Roman rule restricted the power of Jewish courts to carry out executions (John 18:31), and the death penalty for adultery seems rarely to have been enforced.

A public divorce with formal charges, however, would still have brought lasting disgrace. Later Jewish sources indicate that a divorce could be handled quietly, with a written certificate given before witnesses.

20.brief: While Joseph considered these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and told him, as a son of David, not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife, because the child in her was conceived by the Holy Spirit. God Himself answered Joseph’s dilemma and called him to receive Mary and her Son.
20.explain:
“But while he thought about these things,”

Joseph had made his decision, but he had not yet acted on it. He was still turning the matter over. God’s intervention came at the point of decision, before an irreversible step was taken.

“behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream,”

“Behold” draws attention to God’s sudden intervention. An angel is a messenger sent from God. Throughout Matthew’s account of Jesus’ birth and early childhood, God guides Joseph through dreams (1:20; 2:13, 19, 22). Joseph responds each time with immediate obedience.

“saying, ‘Joseph, son of David,”

The angel addresses Joseph by his royal ancestry. Apart from this verse, every use of “son of David” in Matthew refers to Jesus. The title reminds Joseph of who he is and why his role matters. Through Joseph, the son of David, Mary’s child will be received into David’s house.

“do not be afraid to take to you Mary your wife,”

Joseph’s fear may have included the fear of disobeying God’s law, of taking a wife who appeared to have been unfaithful, and of the shame that would follow. The angel removes that fear. “Take to you” means to complete the marriage by bringing Mary into his home. The angel calls her “Mary your wife,” affirming the union Joseph was preparing to end.

“for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit.”

The angel gives the reason Joseph need not fear. Mary has not been unfaithful. The child in her womb has been conceived by the Holy Spirit. What Matthew stated in 1:18, Joseph now learns from God.
20.notes:
Matthew records five revelations given in dreams in chapters 1–2: four to Joseph (1:20; 2:13, 19, 22) and one to the wise men (2:12). A sixth comes later to Pilate’s wife (27:19).

The Greek participle gennēthen, “conceived,” comes from gennaō, the verb translated “begot” throughout the genealogy. Literally, the angel says that which has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit.

The Greek has no article in the expression translated “an angel of the Lord.” Matthew does not name the messenger.

Luke identifies the angel who appeared to Mary as Gabriel (Luke 1:26); Matthew does not name the angel who appeared to Joseph.

21.brief: The angel announces that Mary will bear a Son and that Joseph is to name Him Jesus, “for He will save His people from their sins.” His name declares His mission: He comes to rescue His people from the guilt and rule of sin and restore them to life with God.
21.explain:
“And she will bring forth a Son,”

The angel speaks with certainty about the birth. He does not say, as God said to Abraham and Zacharias, that the woman will bear a son “to you” (Genesis 17:19; Luke 1:13). The child is Mary’s Son and God’s, not Joseph’s by nature.

“and you shall call His name JESUS,”

Naming a child was a father’s right. By giving the child his name, Joseph would publicly acknowledge Jesus as his legal son. “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua (Yeshua or Yehoshua), meaning the LORD saves or the LORD is salvation. It was a common name in Israel, but God chose it for its meaning.

“for He will save His people from their sins.”

The angel explains the name. In Greek, “He” is emphatic: He Himself will save. The Old Testament declares that it is the LORD who will “redeem Israel from all his iniquities” (Psalm 130:8). Now the angel says this child will do what only God can do.

“His people” refers first to Israel, the people to whom Jesus came. As Matthew’s Gospel unfolds, it becomes clear that His people include all who follow Him, from every nation (8:11; 28:19).

“From their sins” defines the salvation He brings. Many in Israel hoped for a Messiah who would deliver them from Roman rule. Jesus came to deliver His people from the guilt and power of sin itself, the deeper bondage behind all their other troubles. He brings forgiveness, freedom from sin’s rule, and restored life with God (Romans 6:1–14; Titus 3:4–7). At the Last Supper He will explain how: “This is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (26:28).
21.notes: In the Septuagint, Joshua’s name is spelled Iēsous, the same Greek name given to Jesus. The KJV twice reads “Jesus” where Joshua is meant (Acts 7:45; Hebrews 4:8).

22.brief: Matthew explains that all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet. The child’s conception and His naming are the outworking of God’s own promise.
22.explain:
“So all this was done”

“All this” gathers together the events of 1:18–21: the conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s distress, the angel’s message, and the command to name the child Jesus. All of it unfolded within God’s purpose.

“that it might be fulfilled”

This is the first of Matthew’s fulfillment statements, which run through his Gospel (for example, 2:15, 17, 23; 4:14; 8:17; 12:17). To “fulfill” means to fill up or bring to completion. Sometimes Jesus fulfills a direct prediction. Sometimes He brings to completion a pattern or promise in Israel’s history. Jesus said He came not to destroy the Law and the Prophets “but to fulfill” them (5:17). Matthew shows that the Old Testament reaches its intended goal in Jesus.

“which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet,”

Matthew distinguishes the speaker from the messenger. The Lord spoke; the prophet was His instrument. The words of Isaiah are the words of God (2 Peter 1:21). The prophet is not named here, but the quotation that follows comes from Isaiah 7:14.

“saying:”

This introduces the quotation in 1:23.
22.notes:
About ten times Matthew introduces Old Testament passages with similar words: “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken.” These statements reflect his purpose of showing that Jesus is the Messiah the Scriptures promised.

Matthew 1:22–23 could be read as the angel’s words continuing, but Matthew uses similar fulfillment statements elsewhere to explain how events fulfill Scripture. These verses are best understood the same way.

23.brief: Matthew cites Isaiah 7:14: “Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and bear a Son, and they shall call His name Immanuel,” which means “God with us.” In the virgin-born Son, God Himself has come to be present with His people.
23.explain:
“Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and bear a Son,”

Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14. “The virgin” translates the Greek word parthenos, which refers to a young woman who has not had sexual relations with a man. Matthew has already made Mary’s virginity clear (1:18, 20) and will state it again in 1:25. The birth of Jesus is the sign God promised.

Isaiah first spoke these words to the house of David in the days of King Ahaz (see 1:9). Jerusalem was under threat, and Ahaz refused to trust the LORD. God gave a sign that carried both a warning and a promise. Isaiah said that before the child would know to refuse evil and choose good, the two kings Ahaz feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:15–16). The prophecy spoke to Ahaz’s own time.

Yet Isaiah’s message about Immanuel does not end in chapter 7. In the following chapters the land of Judah is called “your land, O Immanuel” (Isaiah 8:8), and the prophet announces a Child who will sit on David’s throne and be called “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6–7). No ordinary child of Ahaz’s day could bear those names. Matthew sees the full meaning of Isaiah’s sign in Jesus. He is the only child ever conceived by a virgin, and He is the only one who is truly “God with us.”

“and they shall call His name Immanuel,”

Jesus was not called Immanuel as a personal name. His name, given by the angel, is Jesus. Immanuel describes who He is. “They shall call” refers to those who recognize Him for who He is and confess it. His name, Jesus, tells what He does: He saves. Immanuel tells who He is: God present with His people.

“which is translated, ‘God with us.”

Matthew translates the Hebrew name into Greek. In Jesus, God Himself has come to dwell among His people.

Throughout Scripture God reveals His desire to dwell with His people. He walked with Adam in the garden, filled the tabernacle and the temple with His glory, and promised through the prophets to dwell among His people forever (Ezekiel 37:27). In Jesus that desire reaches its fulfillment. God came Himself, took on human flesh, and lived among His people (John 1:14).

Matthew’s Gospel begins and ends with this truth. Here Jesus is “God with us.” In the middle of the Gospel He promises, “Where two or three are gathered together in My name, I am there in the midst of them” (18:20). In the final verse He tells His disciples, “I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (28:20).
23.notes:
Isaiah 7:14 uses the Hebrew word almah, meaning a young woman of marriageable age. In the Old Testament it describes unmarried young women such as Rebekah (Genesis 24:43) and Moses’ sister, Miriam (Exodus 2:8; compare Numbers 26:59), and no passage clearly uses it of a sexually experienced woman.

The Jewish translators of the Septuagint, working about two centuries before Christ, rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for a virgin.

Some argue that Isaiah would have used betulah if he meant “virgin,” but betulah is not always a precise technical term either, and its use in passages such as Joel 1:8 is debated, so the argument does not settle the question.

Matthew follows the Septuagint, and his own account states plainly that Mary conceived without sexual relations (1:18, 25).

Interpreters differ on whether Isaiah 7:14 had an initial fulfillment in a child born in Ahaz’s time. Proposals include Isaiah’s own son (Isaiah 8:3–4) or a child of the royal family. Hezekiah is sometimes suggested, though the chronology of his reign makes this difficult. Others take the prophecy as speaking directly of the Messiah alone.

The Hebrew text of Isaiah 7:14 is usually read she shall call (the form can also be read “you shall call”), and the Septuagint reads “you shall call.” Matthew’s “they shall call” points to the people who will recognize and confess who Jesus is.

The promise of God’s presence in 1:23 and Jesus’ promise in 28:20 frame the entire Gospel. Writers sometimes used this technique, called an inclusio, to mark a central theme.

24.brief: When Joseph woke, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded and took Mary as his wife. His prompt obedience brought Mary and her Son into his Davidic household.
24.explain:
“Then Joseph, being aroused from sleep,”

Matthew moves straight from the dream to Joseph’s waking. There is no record of delay, debate, or a request for further confirmation.

“did as the angel of the Lord commanded him”

Joseph’s obedience is complete. Scripture records no words from Joseph anywhere in the Gospels. He is known by what he did. The same pattern appears each time God speaks to him: Joseph rises and obeys (2:14, 21).

His obedience likely came at a personal cost. In a small town, people could count the months between the wedding and the birth. Marrying Mary meant that others might assume Joseph was the father of a child conceived before the wedding, or that he had accepted an unfaithful bride. Joseph chose to obey God and to share whatever reproach came to Mary.

“and took to him his wife,”

Joseph brought Mary into his home as his wife. In doing so he gave her his protection and his name, and he took responsibility for her and for the child she carried.
24.notes: The wording of 1:24 closely matches the angel’s command in 1:20: “take to you Mary your wife” becomes “took to him his wife.” Matthew uses the same matching wording when Joseph obeys in 2:13–14 and 2:20–21.

25.brief: Joseph did not have marital relations with Mary until she had given birth to her firstborn Son, and he named Him Jesus. Joseph’s restraint safeguards the virgin birth, and by naming the child he received Him as his own legal son and heir of David’s line.
25.explain:
“and did not know her”

“Know” is the Bible’s way of referring to sexual relations between husband and wife (Genesis 4:1). Although Joseph took Mary into his home, he did not have relations with her during her pregnancy.

“till she had brought forth her firstborn Son.”

Matthew’s statement confirms that Jesus was conceived without a human father. Matthew later names Jesus’ brothers, James, Joses, Simon, and Judas, and mentions His sisters (13:55–56; see also Mark 6:3). In the ordinary reading of the passage, especially when considered alongside the Gospel references to Jesus’ brothers and sisters, the wording most naturally suggests that Joseph and Mary later lived a normal married life.

“Firstborn” marks Jesus as Mary’s first child. In Israel, the firstborn son held a special place of honor and belonged to the LORD in a particular way (Exodus 13:2). The New Testament also uses “firstborn” to describe Jesus’ supremacy over all creation and His resurrection as the first of many who will rise (Colossians 1:15, 18).

“And He called His name JESUS.”

“He” refers to Joseph. Joseph did exactly what the angel commanded in 1:21. By naming the child, Joseph publicly acknowledged Jesus as his son, and through him Jesus took His place in the family of David. The chapter ends with the name that tells who Jesus is and what He came to do: Jesus, the LORD saves.
25.notes:
The Greek conjunction heōs hou (“until”) does not by itself specify what happens after the stated time.

The NKJV reads “her firstborn Son,” following the majority of Greek manuscripts. Several of the oldest manuscripts read simply “a Son.” The word “firstborn” appears without question in Luke’s account of the birth (Luke 2:7).

The verb “did not know” is in the imperfect tense, describing a continuing condition: throughout the months of Mary’s pregnancy, Joseph abstained.
